0: You would hardly guess it: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's very first post on X was devoted to open source.
1: On 24 July 2026 he shared an open letter signed by Nvidia about why open models matter,
2: The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.
3: Many people are used to opening a chat window, sending a question and waiting for the AI to answer. But once you plan to use AI to handle company material over the long term and connect it to internal systems, problems start to appear: is it safe to send the material over? What if the service suddenly rate-limits you? Can the model learn how your company handles its data?
4: Open models offer another way out of these problems. Within what the licence allows, you can download the model, deploy it in your own environment and keep fine-tuning it, letting users decide how it is used.
5: Of course, the open-versus-closed debate over large models has never stopped, and Jensen Huang's letter struck a chord with us too, so we decided to join forces with several contributors and begin this journey of the ModelScope open-model practice cookbook.We bring this open-model practice content to you, and wish the open-model ecosystem a flourishing future ~
7: Chatting with an AI in a browser, or asking a model questions through an API, usually means the vendor runs the model: you send input, they return results, and how the servers are configured or the model maintained is mostly not your concern.
8: Open models offer another choice: you can obtain the trained model parameters — usually called the weights. With suitable software and hardware, those parameters can run on your own computer, server or private cloud. Questions that used to require an external service can then be handled in your own environment.
9: There are two things here that are easy to confuse.
10: Free is about whether you pay; open source is about what you get and how you are allowed to use it. A chat product can be free while not offering model weights. A model you may download for free still needs compute and maintenance to run.
11: An API is only a way of reaching a model. An open model can be hosted by a provider and offered to you through an API; a model you deploy yourself can likewise be served to colleagues through an internal API. So “open or closed” and “call an API or deploy it yourself” should be looked at separately.
12: In everyday discussion people often lump models whose weights can be downloaded together as open models. We will keep using that common shorthand in later chapters.
13: Where it matters we will be precise, though: open weights are not the same as open-sourcing the whole training process. The training data, the training code and the usage permissions each need checking.
15: Once you have a model in hand, you are probably curious about how it was actually learned.
16: That is where the differences between models show: some let you download and run them without publishing the complete training material; others go further and provide training code and data descriptions so outside developers can study how the model was trained.
17: In May 2026 the G7 published a shared reference document on the degree of AI openness, dividing these differences into four classes. From most to least open, they can be understood like this.
18: The complete training data is published too. Model weights, deployment code, training code and the complete training data are all provided under an open licence, corresponding to Open Source AI with Open Data.
19: Weights and code are public, with restricted data fully explained. This corresponds to Open Source AI. The complete training data should in principle be provided; where legal or technical reasons prevent sharing, a thorough data description should take its place.
20: The trained model is handed to you to run and adapt. This corresponds to Open Weights AI, which provides the weights and deployment code under an open licence but not necessarily the complete training material.
21: Downloadable, but with extra conditions on use. This corresponds to Weights Available AI, where the weights and deployment code are available, but the licence may restrict commercial use, regions or specific scenarios.
22: Take Qwen3: the official release provides an open-weight model along with notes on running it locally, deploying, quantizing and fine-tuning it. Developers can run the model with tools such as Transformers, vLLM and SGLang, or keep training it with fine-tuning tools. In the classification above, this reflects the practical value of the open-weights level.
23: Most companies do not need to redo a full pre-training run — running an existing model, adapting it to their own hardware and then fine-tuning it on business samples already solves many concrete business problems.
25: Being able to deploy a model yourself is good, but if it often makes mistakes in business scenarios, it is hard to hand it real work.
26: Open models used to give many people the impression of being convenient for research but a notch below the strongest closed models. As model capabilities keep improving, that judgement needs revisiting.
27: On 18 June 2026 there was an interesting exchange on X. Users were discussing when Chinese models would reach the level of Anthropic's frontier models, and Musk suggested it might take until the first quarter of 2027. Zhipu co-founder Tang Jie replied below with “won't take that long”.
28: Whether their predictions hold depends on how later models perform. What makes the discussion interesting is that open models are already standing at the frontier of large models overall.
29: A security incident Hugging Face disclosed in July 2026 once again showed how much open models matter.
30: Part of HF's production infrastructure was breached, and the security team had to analyse a large volume of attack records to work out what the attackers had done, which credentials they had touched and what was affected. The HF team first tried to use a frontier model through a commercial API and ran into an awkward problem: the real attack commands and exploit content used for the investigation tripped the provider's safety restrictions, and the analysis requests were blocked.
31: The team then carried out the forensic analysis on its own infrastructure using the open-weight model GLM-5.2, which let the investigation continue. The related attack data and credentials also stayed inside the internal environment.
32: In a later technical review, Hugging Face explained further that the team reconstructed around 17,600 attack actions and, with the help of open-weight models including GLM-5.2, decoded obfuscated and encrypted attack payloads
33: This incident shows how much open models matter.
34: Using open models does not have to be constrained the way closed ones are. We can keep the data local, use it even offline, and make task execution far more controllable.
36: Vertical domains are also one of the more important directions for open models. A general large model has learned a great deal of public data, but its understanding of a company's internal device names, business processes, industry terminology and specialist knowledge may still be limited. Fine-tuning on vertical-domain data lets the model learn that specialist knowledge.
37: For tasks that handle sensitive data, local deployment has advantages too. The model can run inference inside the company network and connect to existing knowledge bases, databases and business systems, reducing the need to send sensitive data to external services.
38: Not every task needs a locally deployed open model, however,
39: For tasks that call the model only rarely, change quickly or need to keep using the latest general-model capability, calling an API directly is usually more convenient. For long-term, stable, repeated business tasks, open models have plenty of room to be applied.
40: Tasks such as text classification, intent recognition, information extraction, document summarisation and knowledge-base question answering usually have fairly clear inputs and outputs. A company can pick a model of suitable size for the complexity of the task and train or fine-tune it with its own business data. For tasks like these, the largest model is not necessarily needed.
42: A model runs and performs well, but to use it in a commercial product or share your own fine-tuned version, you still need to check the LICENSE.
43: Being downloadable, being usable commercially and being modifiable and republishable are different permissions.
44: Generally speaking, MIT and Apache License 2.0 are both fairly permissive open-source licences: they allow commercial use and modification and do not require all derivative code to be published. Software under the MIT licence only requires you to keep the copyright and licence notice; Apache 2.0 adds requirements about describing modifications on redistribution, keeping the relevant notices and handling the NOTICE file, and includes an explicit patent grant.
46: Kimi K3 sets separate terms for some commercial uses: deployment, fine-tuning and creating derivative works are allowed, but once the model-service business passes a stated revenue threshold a separate agreement is required.
47: DeepSeek-V3 uses the MIT licence for its code,
48: So when using models, if you want to publish a fine-tuned model or provide it to other users, you need to re-check the original model's licence: whether that use is allowed, and whether you must keep the model name, licence and source information.
49: If a new model is merged from several models, you also need to check each of their licences separately to make sure their requirements do not conflict.
